# Accuracy report - can we trust our numbers?

*Generated by `tools/accuracy_check.py` on 2026-09-21 15:23 UTC. Everything below was recomputed from the raw `.pcap` files in this run (not copied from `metrics.json`). The script only reads the pcaps and writes this file; it does not touch the model.*

## The short version

* **Fair test (VPN settings the model has never seen):** 100.0% of the 180 captures were classified correctly (100.0% of the 1,027 one-second windows). Statistically, with 180/180 correct we can only be 95% sure the true rate is at least 97.9%.
* **But:** those five traffic types come from simple scripts (ping, scp, curl, ffmpeg, SIPp) in one Docker lab. The numbers show the method works **on this lab data**. They do **not** show it would work on real people's traffic, other networks, or other VPN software.
* **Weak spots we found:** the traffic type *file transfer* is the fragile one - with only the first 10 packets of a capture it was missed (file_transfer, 36 of 36 captures) and per-capture accuracy fell to 80%; very heavy timing noise (200 ms) cost 6.5% of captures. And the model has no "unknown" answer: a traffic type it was never taught is forced into one of the five (section 4e).
* The 180-capture end-to-end run (180/180 right) is **not a fair test**: the shipped model was trained on exactly those files. It only proves the whole app (upload → API → model → answer) works.

## 1. What the words mean (plain English)

Imagine a student preparing for an exam.

* **Accuracy** = the percentage of exam questions the student answered correctly. 95 correct out of 100 = 95% accuracy.
* **Fair vs not fair.** If the exam questions were **also in the practice book the student memorised**, a high score proves nothing - they just remembered the answers. The score only means something if the questions are **new**. In our project, the "practice book" is the training data, and a **fair test uses VPN configurations the model never saw while learning**.
* **Per-class accuracy** = the score **per subject**. A student can score 100% in maths and 40% in history; the overall average hides that. Our "subjects" are the five traffic types (web, video, VoIP, file transfer, ping). Per-class accuracy is called *recall*. *Precision* answers the opposite question: when the student writes "history", how often is it really a history question?
* **Confusion matrix** = the marking sheet. Each **row** is what the traffic really was, each **column** is what the model said. A perfect result puts every number on the diagonal (top-left to bottom-right). A number off the diagonal shows which type was mistaken for which - e.g. "video mistaken for web".
* **Unseen configuration** = a VPN setting combination (cipher × Diffie-Hellman group × tunnel/transport × PFS label) that was completely kept out of training. We have 36 configurations; the test always uses a group of them that the model did not train on.

### Which of our numbers are FAIR and which are NOT

| Number | Fair? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Grouped cross-validation, 100.0% per capture / 100.0% per window (section 2; also in `metrics.json`) | **FAIR** | every test configuration was hidden during training |
| Leave-one-configuration-out, leave-one-cipher-out, leave-one-DH-group-out (section 2) | **FAIR (stricter)** | hides even more: a whole cipher or DH group the model never met |
| Robustness tests (a)-(e) (section 4) | **FAIR** | test configurations are unseen; only the *test* data is damaged |
| Shuffled-label control (section 5) | control | not an accuracy claim; it shows what pure guessing looks like |
| 180-capture end-to-end run through `/analyze` (180/180 correct) | **NOT FAIR** | the shipped model was trained on these same 180 captures (like re-taking an exam you studied) |
| The **old** "100%" from before the fix | **NOT FAIR** | random split: near-copies of the same capture were in both training and test; it also used the packet count, which gives the answer away |
| "Capture length alone = 100%" (section 5) | fair but *bad news* | proves the old feature was a shortcut - which is why it was removed |

**A remaining limit even for the fair numbers:** "unseen configuration" means new VPN *settings*, but the test captures were produced by the **same scripts, in the same lab, with the same tools** as the training captures. There is one capture per (configuration, traffic type) - no repeated runs.

## 3. All 180 captures through the real app path - NOT an unseen-data test

Every capture was uploaded to the real `POST /analyze` endpoint (same code path as the website: IKE parser → ML model → answer; called through FastAPI's built-in test client, so no network port is involved) and compared with the ground truth in `manifest.csv`.

> ⚠️ **This is NOT a fair accuracy test.** The shipped model (`ml-engineer/models/traffic_classifier.pkl`) was trained on windows from **these same 180 files**. It is the student re-taking the exam they studied. What it *does* prove: the whole pipeline works end to end, with no crashes or format problems, and the model at least reproduces its own training data.

**Result: 180 of 180 correct (100.0%), 0 HTTP errors, 230 s total.**

| True class | Captures | Correct | Lowest confidence | Average confidence |

## 4. Robustness: what happens when the data is damaged? (all on unseen configurations)

Method: the models are the six cross-validation models from section 2 (each trained on clean data from other configurations). Only the **test** captures are damaged before being classified. "Per-capture" = one answer per capture (windows averaged). Some damage leaves a capture with no usable window (fewer than 2 packets in every second) - the app would say "too sparse to classify". The table therefore gives accuracy **on the captures that could be classified**, and the stricter number where a refusal counts as wrong.

| Test | Per-window accuracy | Per-capture accuracy (of those classified) | Per-capture, refusals count as wrong | Captures classified | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sanity: nothing damaged | 100.0% | 100.0% | 100.0% | 100% | must equal section 2 |
| (a) only the first 5 seconds | 100.0% | 100.0% | 100.0% | 100% | file transfer, VoIP and video are already under 5 s; only web and ping shrink (windows 1,027 to 507) |
| (b) only the first 10 packets | 88.8% | 80.0% | 80.0% | 100% |  |
| (c) randomly drop 20% of packets (5 random runs) | 98.2% | 100.0% | 100.0% | 100% | worst run 100.0% |
| (d) timing jitter, sd 10 ms (3 runs) | 99.8% | 100.0% | 100.0% | 100% | worst run 100.0% |
| (d) timing jitter, sd 50 ms (3 runs) | 99.2% | 99.8% | 99.8% | 100% | worst run 99.4% |
| (d) timing jitter, sd 200 ms (3 runs) | 97.2% | 93.5% | 93.5% | 100% | worst run 92.2% |

* Mistakes in (b) first 10 packets, by true class (summed over runs): file_transfer: 36
* Mistakes in (d) jitter 50 ms, by true class (summed over runs): file_transfer: 1
* Mistakes in (d) jitter 200 ms, by true class (summed over runs): file_transfer: 35

Jitter is Gaussian noise added to every packet timestamp. sd 10 ms is realistic Internet variation; 200 ms is severe. (The lab captures are on a local Docker network with almost no natural jitter, so real networks are a genuine unknown.)

### (e) What happens with a traffic type the model was never taught?

For each of the 5 classes in turn, the model was trained on the **other four** (on unseen-config folds) and then shown captures of the missing class. A model that only knows 4 answers **must** pick one of them; the question is whether it at least sounds unsure.

| Class left out | Accuracy on the 4 known classes | The unknown captures were labelled as... | Confidence on unknown | Confidence on known | Unknown flagged as unsure (<60%) | Known flagged (false alarm) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| file_transfer | 100.0% | video_streaming: 36 | 71% | 100% | 0% | 0% |
| icmp | 100.0% | web_browsing: 36 | 59% | 99% | 53% | 0% |
| video_streaming | 100.0% | file_transfer: 19, web_browsing: 10, voip: 7 | 41% | 100% | 100% | 0% |
| voip | 100.0% | video_streaming: 27, web_browsing: 9 | 47% | 99% | 100% | 0% |
| web_browsing | 100.0% | video_streaming: 36 | 54% | 99% | 81% | 0% |

Reading it: the model has **no "I don't know" answer** - a traffic type it was never taught is forced into one of the known classes (shown in the third column). The good news is that it sounds much less sure: average confidence is 41%-71% on unknown types versus about 100% on known ones, and the app's "Low classification confidence" warning (below 60%) never fired on known types (no false alarms). The bad news is that the warning is unreliable at catching unknowns: it caught file_transfer 0%, icmp 53%, video_streaming 100%, voip 100%, web_browsing 81% of the missing type's captures, so for **file_transfer** most unknown captures slipped through with a fairly confident wrong label. **The model must not be trusted on traffic types outside these five** (e.g. games, DNS floods, torrents, real video calls).

## 5. Leakage checks: is the model cheating?

### The exact features the model sees

Twelve numbers per 1-second window of ESP packets, computed only from packet **sizes, arrival times and direction**:

| # | Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `pkts_per_sec` | how many packets per second |
| 2 | `bytes_per_sec` | data rate (bytes per second) |
| 3 | `mean_size` | average packet size |
| 4 | `std_size` | variation in packet sizes |
| 5 | `min_size` | smallest packet size |
| 6 | `max_size` | largest packet size |
| 7 | `median_size` | typical (median) packet size |
| 8 | `mean_inter_arrival` | average gap between packets |
| 9 | `std_inter_arrival` | variation in the gap between packets |
| 10 | `max_inter_arrival` | longest pause between packets |
| 11 | `fwd_packet_ratio` | share of packets sent in the first direction |
| 12 | `fwd_byte_ratio` | share of bytes sent in the first direction |

* The features used in this audit are **identical** to the ones inside the shipped model file (`feature_names_in_`): **True**.
* Check that none of these are features: `packet_count, total_bytes, duration, duration_sec, filename, file, combo, run, label, cipher, dh, mode, pfs, n_packets, n_bytes, window_index, start_offset_sec` → **all absent**.

### File names and run numbers

* The feature code never receives a file name - it reads packets only. To prove it end to end, 15 captures (3 per class) were uploaded to `/analyze` under **three different names** (the real name, `capture.pcap`, `zz_run99_qwerty.pcap`): the traffic answer **and all five class probabilities were identical for 15 of 15** files.
* Run numbers: every capture is `run1` (there is exactly one run per configuration and class), so run-to-run variation cannot be tested at all - it is a gap, not a pass. The model cannot use the run number because it is not a feature.

### Capture length

* Capture length is **not** a feature (no packet count, byte total or duration). Why it matters: a one-number model that only knows *how many packets the file has* scores **100.0%** on unseen configurations, because the lab stopped `tcpdump` after a fixed number of packets per traffic type: file_transfer 3742-5000, icmp 12-18, video_streaming 323-500, voip 27-30, web_browsing 215-300. That is the shortcut the first model used.
* Our model is not riding on it. In test (b) every capture is cut to **10 packets**, which erases capture-length information (every capture is then the same length). Accuracy falls to 80% - so length is not the *only* cue - but it does not fall to chance (20%): the four other classes are still classified correctly and only file_transfer, 36 of 36 captures fails. That failure is honest information, not leakage: ten packets of a large file transfer look like a tiny exchange.

### Shuffled-label control (should be chance level)

Each capture was given the label of a *random other capture* and the whole grouped cross-validation was repeated 5 times. If the pipeline secretly leaked answers, accuracy would stay high. It should fall to guessing:

| Repeat | Per-capture accuracy | Per-capture balanced accuracy | Per-window accuracy | Per-window balanced accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 18.3% | 18.3% | 17.4% | 17.2% |
| 1 | 22.2% | 22.2% | 20.0% | 18.7% |
| 2 | 22.2% | 22.2% | 22.9% | 22.3% |
| 3 | 19.4% | 19.4% | 20.7% | 20.0% |
| 4 | 15.6% | 15.6% | 17.6% | 17.2% |
| **average** | **19.6%** | **19.6%** | **19.7%** | **19.1%** |

Pure guessing among 5 balanced classes = **20%**; the always-answer-'web' strategy scores 59.5% of windows (web dominates the windows). Our shuffled results (19.6% per capture, balanced accuracy 19.6%) sit at chance level, versus 100.0% with the real labels. So the 100%-type results come from real structure in the packet sizes and timing, not from a hidden leak in the pipeline.

## 6. Verdict

### What is proven

* On unseen VPN configurations (new cipher / DH group / mode / PFS-label combinations, even a whole unseen cipher), the classifier separated the **five lab traffic types** almost perfectly: **100.0% per capture, 100.0% per second-window**, across several different splits and leave-one-out tests.
* The result is **not** caused by file names, run numbers or the capture length as such, and is **not** a pipeline leak: shuffled labels drop to chance, and the app gives identical answers when the same file is uploaded under a different name.
* The classifier tolerates moderate damage to the data: 20% of packets missing → 100.0% per capture, 10 ms timing jitter → 100.0%, 50 ms → 99.8%, first 5 seconds only → 100.0% (refusals counted as wrong).
* Its weak spots are now **known and measured**: only 10 packets → 80.0% (file_transfer, 36 of 36 captures missed), 200 ms jitter → 93.5%, and unknown traffic types are forced into a known class.
* The whole app pipeline works end to end on all 180 captures (180/180; a plumbing check, not an accuracy claim).

### What is NOT proven

* **Real-world traffic.** The five classes are made by scripts (ping, scp, curl, ffmpeg range requests, SIPp signalling without audio). Real browsing, video calls, cloud sync or games were never tested.
* **Other networks.** All captures come from one Docker network with almost no delay, jitter or loss. Real Wi-Fi/mobile/Internet paths change timing and packet sizes.
* **Other VPN software.** Only strongSwan (Linux, ESP) was tested; WireGuard, OpenVPN, Windows/Cisco IPsec, NAT-T and different MTUs are unknown.
* **Traffic types outside the five.** The model cannot say "I don't know" (section 4e); it will pick one of the five.
* **Repeatability.** Only one capture per configuration and class exists; run-to-run variation is untested. Captures were stopped by packet count, so file-transfer, VoIP and video captures are under 2 s long (1-2 windows each) - the model has seen very few examples of them.
* **The security score.** This report covers only the traffic classifier. The cipher/DH values for the lab captures come from the file names ("declared"), because none of the 216 captures contains a readable IKE_SA_INIT; the IKE parser has only been tested on synthetic messages.
* **Statistical precision.** 180 captures (36 per class, from 36 configurations that differ only in a few settings) give a limited estimate: even a perfect score only guarantees, at 95% confidence, a true rate of at least about 97.9% *for this kind of lab data*.

### What to say to the judges

> "We tested our traffic classifier the strict way: every VPN configuration in the test was completely hidden from the model, and it still got 100% of our lab captures right. We checked it isn't cheating: it never sees file names or capture length, and with shuffled labels it falls to plain guessing. We also stress-tested it, and it holds up with 20% of packets missing and normal timing noise, though it struggles with only ten packets and can't say 'I don't know' to traffic it was never taught. Our data comes from scripted tests in one lab, so we claim it works for these five traffic types, not yet for real-world traffic or other VPN products - and we fixed an earlier inflated score, so we only report fair numbers."
